label: Three Views Compared
title: What happens to the unrepentant?
intro: Two views sit inside evangelical bounds and differ over what final punishment is. A third, universalism, is shown for contrast because evangelical statements reject it.
image_title: Three views of final judgment, compared
image_subtitle: Universalism is shown for contrast; evangelical statements reject it.
image_subtitle_narrow: Universalism is shown for contrast; evangelical statements reject it.
caption: Eternal conscious torment and conditional immortality both teach a real, final judgment from which there is no return. They part over whether the lost go on existing under punishment or are finally destroyed. Universalism holds that God will at last save everyone.
image_source: Sources: Denny Burk (TGC); Edward Fudge (JETS); Robin Parry; Evangelical Alliance UK, The Nature of Hell (2000)

common_text: Both evangelical views affirm a real and final judgment, and the Evangelical Alliance's report counts the debate between them "a secondary rather than a primary issue for evangelical theology."
differ: Duration: punishment that goes on forever, or a punishment whose result, destruction, lasts forever.
Immortality: conditionalists hold that life without end is God's gift to the saved, not a property of every soul.
Matthew 25:46: "eternal punishment" read as unending experience by traditionalists and as a final, irreversible outcome by conditionalists.
Universalism: neither evangelical view accepts it; the Evangelical Alliance report rejects it outright.

sources.title: Hell as Endless Punishment
sources.quote: Hell is a place of eternal, conscious torment for everyone who does not trust in Jesus Christ.
sources.notes: Denny Burk, Concise Theology essay, September 10, 2020. Also: "Eternal conscious torment has been the majority position of the Christian church throughout its 2,000-year history." Texts include Matthew 25:46, Mark 9:43 to 48, Revelation 20:10. Confessional statements of the view: Westminster Confession 33.2 ("cast into eternal torments", https://www.opc.org/wcf.html) and Baptist Faith and Message 2000, Article X ("the place of everlasting punishment", https://bfm.sbc.net/bfm2000/).

sources.publisher: Journal of the Evangelical Theological Society
sources.title: The Final End of the Wicked
sources.quote: It is rather of what that punishment consists.
sources.notes: Edward Fudge, JETS 27/3 (September 1984), hosted on his own site. Preceding sentence: the question "is not, therefore, whether the wicked will suffer eternal punishment". Cites 2 Thessalonians 1:9 ("everlasting destruction"). Rethinking Hell's Statement on Evangelical Conditionalism (https://rethinkinghell.com/statement/, 2019): life "will ultimately be granted forever to the saved and revoked forever from the unsaved", citing Romans 2:7 and Matthew 10:28.

sources.title: 7 Myths about Christian Universalism
sources.quote: So it is not hell that universalists deny so much as certain views about hell.
sources.notes: Robin Parry, author of The Evangelical Universalist (as Gregory MacDonald). Also: universalists believe God wants to save all people and "God will achieve that goal." Texts: Romans 5:18; 1 Corinthians 15:22; Colossians 1:20; Philippians 2:11.

sources.title: The Nature of Hell
sources.quote: is a significant minority evangelical view
sources.notes: ACUTE report, ed. David Hilborn. Para 18: eternal conscious punishment "represents the classic, mainstream evangelical position". Para 19 (quoted): conditional immortality "is a significant minority evangelical view" and the debate "should be regarded as a secondary rather than a primary issue for evangelical theology." Also: "We also reject the teaching of universalism". Landing page: https://www.eauk.org/church/resources/theological-articles/the-nature-of-hell.cfm
